title: "Fire broke out in a two-story brick stable at No. 1726 Prairie avenue, owned by James R. Walker…"
creator: Chicago Daily Tribune (fire news)
collection: The Chicago Daily Tribune, Feb. 27, 1893 (vol. 52 no. 58)
found_via: IA full-text search '"1726 prairie"'; OCR passage read (clean)
notes: "…at 3:25 o'clock yesterday afternoon. The horses and carriages were quickly removed and were not injured. The loss on the building is estimated at $150." A TWO-STOREY BRICK STABLE stood behind 1726 in 1893, with minor damage only — it would still be there in 1904 (the 1911 Sanborn shows a 2-storey brick house at 1726; rear not noted). Owner and occupant James Ransom Walker, listed at 1726 in the Blue Books 1890–1915 (incl. 1904) — distinct from Mrs. James M. Walker at 1720 (Blue Books 1891–1915), which bears on the library's 'Tyrrell / James Walker' identification of 1720. A Tribune ad of Apr. 22, 1886 (page n5) offered '1726 Prairie-av.—10 rooms; choice location' to rent. CONFLICT with the library: id 51 calls the 1726–1728 building a frame double house demolished in the 1880s, but the chicagology texts (brick 14-room house 1875; 'double-swell brick houses' 1898) and these notices show a BRICK house at 1726 continuously occupied 1875–1915. Either id 51 is a different, earlier building, or the 1904 house at 1726 needs its own record.
rights_basis: Published in the United States before 1929

title: Building permits: 'Gen. Strong, two-story and basement brick, 23x32 feet, at 882 Prairie avenue.'
creator: Chicago Daily Tribune (building-permits list)
collection: Chicago Daily Tribune, Aug. 8, 1875, image 8
found_via: loc.gov Chronicling America search '"882 prairie"' (Chicago); OCR read, then the line read on the page image (OCR gives 'Gen. Shoos … 23 iS2')
notes: Permit to General Henry Strong (owner of old 882 / 1736 Prairie 1876–80, who sold to Hugh McBirney in Dec. 1880 — chicagology) for a TWO-STOREY AND BASEMENT BRICK building 23 ft wide [depth read as 32 ft on the image; the second digit is faint — 32 or possibly 52]. The 23-ft width fits the 27 11/12-ft corner lot at 18th Street, and the date matches the page's lifespan '1875–1912'; so the house McBirney bought in 1880, and which he occupied until his death there in Nov. 1910 (Tribune Nov. 16, 1910; Blue Book 1904 'McBirney Hugh, 1736 Prairie av.'), is most likely this 1875 Strong house, not an 1864 Ingraham house. The 1911 Sanborn draws 1736 as 3 storeys + basement brick — a later added storey or a mansard counted as a storey (the library already notes 'mansard may be later addition'). CONFLICT: the collection's AABN 1889 permit 'H. J. McBirney, three-st'y dwell., Prairie Ave.' (dw-aabn-1889-mcbirney-1736-permit) is assigned to 1736, but Hugh J. McBirney (the son) is listed at 1625 Prairie in every Blue Book 1891–1910 while his father Hugh stays at 1736 — the 1889 Burling & Whitehouse house is 1625, agreeing with the reattribution of the Art Institute 'McBirney' plate to 1625.

title: "Charles M. Henderson's Residence Partly Burned. Fire Breaks Out While All the Family but a Daughter Are at a Concert… Damage $10,000, Largely to Wardrobe…"
creator: Chicago Sunday Tribune (front page)
collection: The Chicago Sunday Tribune, Dec. 8, 1895 (vol. 54 no. 342)
found_via: IA full-text search '"1816 prairie"'; OCR article read (djvu text)
notes: Fire in the Henderson house 'shortly after 10 o'clock last night', damage about $10,000, 'nearly one-half' of it to Mrs. Henderson's wardrobe; pictures, tapestries and bric-a-brac damaged by the firemen. Miss Bessie Henderson was in her room on the SECOND FLOOR; four servant girls in another part of the house; the fire began on the lower floor. An interior fire with no structural loss reported — the house was repaired and the widow lived there until the 1920s (Tribune society notes 1896–1921; tax list July 4, 1903). So the 1873 Henderson house stood in 1904 with Mrs. C. M. Henderson as occupant; the library's 'unresolved' can be closed. Henderson died at 1816 on Jan. 23, 1896 and left the widow 'the homestead at No. 1816 Prairie avenue, the household furniture, and horses' (Tribune Feb. 8, 1896).
